lead: MAYDAY is the one call that stops all other traffic and sets a rescue going. It has a fixed form so that you can say it under stress and anyone who hears it can write it down. Learn the form by heart.

qa.q: When is a problem at sea serious enough to call MAYDAY?
qa.a: When a vessel or a person is in **grave and imminent danger** and needs immediate assistance: the danger is serious and here now, like a fire out of control or a hull the pumps cannot keep up with. Call at once; anyone aboard may.

blocks.p: **MAYDAY** is the distress signal. It says that a vessel or a person is in **grave and imminent danger** and needs **immediate assistance**. Both halves must be true: the danger is serious, and it is here now. When they are, call at once. Do not wait for the yacht to strike the rocks.

head: Situation
MAYDAY?
rows: Holed, the pumps cannot keep up
Yes: a life is in danger
No engine, anchor dragging on to a lee shore
Engine will not start, calm sea, sails working
No: sail on, or make a lower-priority call

blocks.p: In distress **anyone aboard** may use the radio. The rule that an operator needs a certificate never stops a MAYDAY, so show every crew member where the set is and how the call goes.

sections.title: The red button, then your voice on 16

qa.q: How do I send a MAYDAY on a DSC radio?
qa.a: Lift the cover and hold the **red distress button** for five seconds, then on channel 16, high power, say MAYDAY three times, THIS IS, the yacht's name three times, and her call sign or MMSI.

blocks.p: On a DSC set, start with the red button: lift the cover and hold it for five seconds. The alert goes out as data and the set moves to **channel 16**. Check that it is on high power, press the switch on the handset and speak slowly and clearly. First comes the **distress call**, which says who is in trouble.
MAYDAY three times, THIS IS, the yacht's name three times, then her call sign or MMSI. Do not stop there: the message follows without a pause.

sections.title: What rescuers need, in the order they need it

qa.q: What do I say in a MAYDAY message, and in what order?
qa.a: The **distress message** runs: MAYDAY and your name, position, what is wrong, the help you need, the number of persons on board, other useful information, OVER. Position comes first, so help can set out even if the radio dies.

blocks.p: The **distress message** opens with MAYDAY and the name once more. **Position comes first**: if the radio dies ten seconds later, help can still set out. Then what is wrong, what help you need and how many people are aboard.

head: Letter
Item
rows: Information that helps: liferaft, flares, hull colour

blocks.p: Under stress people forget the help they need and the number aboard. Keep a card with the form, the yacht's name, call sign and MMSI beside the radio.

sections.title: Coordinates, or a bearing from a charted mark

qa.q: How do I give my position in a MAYDAY without GPS?
qa.a: Give a **true bearing from** a charted mark, such as a lighthouse, and your distance off: your bearing to the mark plus or minus 180°. A light bearing 040° puts you 220° from it.

blocks.p: With a GPS, read the coordinates: **latitude first, then longitude**, each with its hemisphere, north or south, east or west. Without one, give a **true bearing from** a charted point and the distance off: a lighthouse or a headland that rescuers will find on their own chart.

fig.note: Bearing taken from your boat to the light

blocks.cap: You say: "220 degrees from the lighthouse, 3 miles".

blocks.p: The bearing you take runs from your boat to the mark. Rescuers plot the other way, from the mark out to you, so give the **reciprocal**: add or subtract 180°. The light bears 040°, so you are 220° from it.

blocks.rule: From the landmark, not to it: your bearing plus or minus 180°.

qa.q: What do I do if nobody answers my MAYDAY?
qa.a: Check channel 16 and high power, repeat the call and the message, and raise the alarm by flares and the EPIRB. When a station answers **RECEIVED MAYDAY**, help is being organised: answer briefly and stay on 16.

blocks.p: End the message with **OVER**, release the switch and listen on 16. A coast station or a vessel nearby acknowledges:
**RECEIVED MAYDAY** means your distress call has been heard and help is being organised. The station then asks what it still needs: answer briefly and stay on 16.

list: No answer: check channel 16 and high power, then repeat the call and the message.
Meanwhile raise the alarm by every other means you have: flares, the EPIRB.
The danger has passed and you need no help: tell the coast station at once. Rescuers keep coming until they are told.
Abandoning ship: take the handheld VHF into the liferaft, so you can talk to rescuers as they close in.

sections.title: Calling for a vessel that cannot

qa.q: When should I send a MAYDAY RELAY for another boat?
qa.a: Send a **MAYDAY RELAY** when you hear a MAYDAY that no station acknowledges and you cannot help yourself, or when you see a distress signal, like a red flare, from a vessel silent on the radio. Call under your own name.

blocks.p: Sometimes the casualty reaches nobody, and you can. Send a **MAYDAY RELAY** in two cases: you hear a MAYDAY that no station acknowledges and you cannot give the help yourself; or you see a distress signal, such as a red flare, from a vessel that is silent on the radio.

fig.note: Night · red parachute flare, nothing heard on 16

blocks.p: Each of the three is said three times, like MAYDAY itself, and you call under **your own name**. Never pose as the casualty: rescuers must know who is speaking and where the message comes from. Then pass on her position and trouble as you heard them, or say what you saw, where and when.
